analysis.answer: Current law allows parents of eligible children to open an education savings account funded at 90 percent of the state's per-pupil funding, which can be used for private tuition, tutoring, textbooks, and online courses. The measure repeals this program effective July 1, 2028, and transfers any remaining account balances back to the state school fund.

The state saves the administrative costs of the program and no longer transfers 90 percent of per-pupil funding to private accounts. However, if students using the accounts return to public schools, the state will pay the full 100 percent per-pupil cost, potentially increasing direct state spending. Families lose the financial subsidy and face the direct cost of paying for private education out of pocket.

Public school districts benefit by retaining full per-pupil funding and receiving any reverted account balances. Families currently using the program bear the cost of losing the financial subsidy for their children's education. Private schools, tutors, and educational vendors lose the revenue previously provided by the accounts.

Families may respond by withdrawing their children from private or alternative education and enrolling them in public schools. Private schools and tutoring services may experience enrollment declines and reduced revenue. Public schools will need to accommodate an influx of returning students.

The measure addresses the diversion of public funds to private entities and the administrative complexity of managing individual accounts. However, by eliminating the program, it creates a barrier for families seeking educational alternatives, potentially leading to financial shortages for lower-income parents who cannot afford private options without state support.
Public school districts and state education agencies gain power, funding, and enrollment as resources are consolidated back into the traditional public school system.

Researchers disagree on the fiscal and educational impacts of education savings accounts and voucher programs. Some studies find they save taxpayer money because the voucher amount is less than the cost of public school, while others find they drain public budgets by subsidizing students who would have attended private school anyway. Evidence on whether such programs improve or harm student achievement is also disputed.
Administration and enforcement costs will decrease as the state no longer has to manage or audit individual education savings accounts.
This is a statutory measure that can be amended or repealed by a future legislature.

flags.note: The repeal takes effect on July 1, 2028, giving the program a phase-out period.
